Package org.aeonbits.owner.validation

Interface ConfigValidator

All Known Implementing Classes:
BeanValidator
public interface ConfigValidator
Checks the constraint annotations of a configuration, which the core can see but cannot check.

Implementations are found through ServiceLoader, declared in META-INF/services/org.aeonbits.owner.validation.ConfigValidator, exactly as Loader is. owner-extras ships one for Bean Validation; this interface is here so that it can be shipped from outside the dependency-free core, and it is public so that anyone with another idea of what a constraint means can put one in its place.

What it is called with, and what it is not

Only the properties that carry a constraint and that the library was willing to read arrive here, each with its value already obtained - see ConstrainedProperty. A configuration with no constraint annotation on it never reaches a validator at all, which is what keeps this free for everybody who is not using it.

The shapes that are left out are left out by the library and not by the validator, and none of them is left out quietly: they are reported, and refused outright under owner.strict. A method taking arguments has no key until it is called and nobody knows what to call it with; a default method is the user's own code rather than a property; an accessor returning a nested interface answers with a view of the properties, which is never null and never absent, so a constraint on it could not fail. A constraint written on a method returning an Optional or a collection is checked against the container, which is likewise never absent - Optional<@Min(12) Integer> is the spelling that says something - and that too is reported rather than left to look like a check.

What is expected back

Every violation found, not the first: a configuration is read once at startup and being told all of it at once is the difference between one restart and five. That is the shape MissingMandatoryPropertyException already has, and the two are answering the same question about the same file.

A validator that cannot run at all - its API is there, since the constraints resolved, but no provider is - must say so by throwing, naming what is missing and what to add, rather than returning no violations. Returning none is the answer that means "these constraints hold", and it is not something to say when nothing was checked.

  • Method Details

    • validate

      List<Violation> validate(List<ConstrainedProperty> properties)
      Checks the given properties against the constraints their methods declare.
      Parameters:
      properties - the properties to check, never empty.
      Returns:
      the violations found, in no particular order; an empty list when every constraint holds.
      Throws:
      UnsupportedOperationException - if the constraints cannot be checked at all, for instance because no validation provider is on the class path.
